utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May I ask Madam Registrar, please, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, after re-examining yesterday's transcript, it has to be emphasised that it is for the Trial Chamber and solely for the Trial Chamber to intervene in such cases where they believe that a question is not based on evidence or other admissible material or, to put it the other way around, that a question is absolutely unbased or out of the blue. Therefore, Mr. Lukic, we regard your question when the witness was asked whether or not persons were dismissed by the Crisis Staff, and you intervened at that time asking the other counsel to present a document in which the Crisis Staff is firing people on the basis of the admitted evidence, this intervention only can be called a frivolous objection. And please refrain from doing so in the future. May I ask now the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. We hope you feel well today, and the same rules apply as yesterday, especially now when you are sitting far away and I can't really see whether you have a problem or not. Please, immediately tell us when you need a break. May I ask, Mr. Koumjian, please, to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, could the witness be provided with the following documents, S77, S178, and S308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday and beginning on page 12 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked some questions by Mr. Lukic about whether you know if the army or the police, did they get their salaries from the municipality or from the republic, or in the case of the army, from the federal state prior to that period. Sir, it's a well-known fact, is it not, that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was paying the salary of officers of the former JNA, the army of Republika Srpska, up until just a very short time ago, within the last couple years. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. The officers of the former JNA who were on the territory of Republika Srpska or Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, and who originate from that area, who are the natives of that area, I believe that they were paid from that source up until two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And unless it's necessary, I won't read all of your answer because it's rather lengthy, it continues on page 13. But you indicated that the budget for the soldiers was not paid by the municipality except for budget for families of soldiers. I'll start reading on page 13, line 9. Just to be complete, I'll start reading from page 13, line 3: "I'm certain that the army was paid and supplied from the budget of the former Yugoslavia or from the Republic budget. They did have a number of privileges for the same reason. That's prior to 1992, the same system continued in 1992, 1991, 1992, and 1993. Probably even after that. I must point out that in 1994, there was a situation that represented a small aberration from what I was telling you about. The Executive Board in 1994 secured part of the budget funds from part of the budget for the families of soldiers who had been on the front. I think this can be traced to the documents of the Municipal Assembly." And then you continued - and I'm interested in this last sentence, sir - and said: "As for the MUP, I don't think I can give you a precise answer. I suppose that they were probably paid from the budget, but I noted the MUP was not paid from the municipal budget in 1994." I have three documents I'd like to show you, given that you indicated you had some uncertainty. The first is S77. Sir, you'll see it's signed by Dr. Stakic, and you've already told us who Ranko Travar was and Simo Drljaca. Do you know Radovan Rajlic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was his position in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a soldier in the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the first paragraph, sir, you'll see that it indicates conclusion, Simo Drljaca, Ranko Travar, and Radovan Rajlic are charged with making a comprehensive review of the possibilities and set criteria and recommendations to the Crisis Staff -- and recommending to the Crisis Staff a manner of payment to and catering for the army and the police in the Prijedor Municipality. And this is dated the 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put the English version always at the same time on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, that was 77A would be the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, while that's being done, isn't it correct that Mr. Travar was secretary for the economy of the municipality and a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before I get your comments, I'll show you all three documents once Your Honours have had a better chance to read through the one that's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just indicate to me when you're ready. Okay, if we could now have S308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document - please take your time and review it - dated the 5th of June, 1992. On the bottom, it's indicated it's signed by the president, Dr. Milomir Stakic. And among the addressees on the bottom left are all enterprises, organisations, and sociopolitical communities. I don't think it's necessary to read the entire document. I'll just read the first sentence. The conclusion is on the method of calculation and payment of salaries and enterprises, organisations, and sociopolitical communities for the month of May. And then I'll just direct your attention to the paragraph below number 4 which states: "Employees serving in the military and police units will not receive their salaries from the cashier unless they produce a certificate issued by the competent military command, Zarko Zrenjanin barracks - forgive my pronunciation - or the Prijedor public security station." Now, the last document, if we're ready to move on, would be S178. And I ask that be put on last because it's dated the 20th of March, 1996. Sir, in March 1996, was Milomir Stakic again holding the position of president of the Municipal Assembly, in March of 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, I believe that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We understand that exact dates are difficult to recall. Sir, this document indicates that it's an extract from the minutes of an extraordinary session of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly Defence council. My first question to you is: What was the Prijedor Municipal Assembly Defence council, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Among those who attended this meeting which occurred according to the date after the Dayton agreement was Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the Municipal Assembly; Pero Colic, assistant commander of operations group 10; Lieutenant-Colonel Radovan Smitran, commander of the 43rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade; Major Radovan Ilic, commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade; and Slavko Budimir, chief of the Ministry of Defence section. It appears the meeting was chaired by Dr. Stakic, and discussed several issues. In the interests of time, I am just going to try to just select parts of those. If counsel likes, I can read the rest. Item number 2 on page 3 of the English, and for your benefit, sir, I believe that's conclusions number 2, "representatives of the army must send in writing all requests regarding army requirements, finances, land, buildings, flats, building and other types of material and equipment to the Prijedor Municipality executive committee. Requests must be specific and itemised." And I'm going to skip down to number 6: "Representatives of the army shall be recommended to retain as much as possible the vehicles classified as war booty, particularly those that are special purpose. They should be stored and lent for temporary use by enterprises in the municipality according to special procedures." And then number 7: "Bearing in mind the serious material situation in the municipality, the municipality could temporarily provide pay for a maximum of 1.000 to 1200 members of the army." Sir, having reviewed these three documents, would you agree with me that the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor under Dr. Stakic and the Crisis Staff did work on matters of salaries and pay for the army and the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to elaborate a bit, and I will comment on the statement that I issued yesterday. I was talking about the period between October 1993 and 1st of August, 1994. And when I was the president of the Executive Board, I did not have the payment records. If this happened at the time, I don't know. But these documents belong to an earlier period which I couldn't know about these things. The second thing is very important, and that is that all this time, we were in the conditions of an immediate threat of war, and this war was declared in 1995. I cannot quote any of the laws from that time, but I know how I was supposed to behave. Companies were supposed to pay salaries to their workers who were militarily engaged, and the army was supposed to reimburse that. I don't think that we were ever reimbursed. I don't know what the situation was in 1992 in terms of reimbursement. In 1996, I believe that Mr. Stakic was the president. The Dayton Accords which were signed on the 21st of December, 1995, we all know what happened then. According to the Dayton Accords, I believe that the army belonged to different entities, and the Republika Srpska had the right to have their army. There was the delineation between the Bosnia and Herzegovina federation and Republika Srpska. And then the conditions were being put in place, please understand me when I say that. I am just assuming, and that doesn't mean that this is correct. At that time, Republika Srpska could not have a budget from which to pay the army. For that reason, I assume that the 43rd Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade, and I believe that it says here in the text that people should be demobilised to the largest possible extent, I believe that for that reason, a decision was made that this should be paid from the municipality or that municipality would be the provider for that part of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, based on your experience as a leading businessman; as, for a while, a member of the government; and having served in the armed forces first in the time of the federal republic; and later during the wars after the breakup of Yugoslavia, would you agree with me that the concept of all people's defence as the name implies calls for a close coordination between the military, the civilians, and the business sector all in furtherance of a united war effort? Is that the idea of "all people's defence"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to comment on that because I was not familiar with the laws at that time. But what I can say, that all people's defence implied different conditions. I hope you won't mind when I say that this was the concept of Defence that prevailed in the entire Yugoslavia. This concept could not continue in view of the secession of Slovenia and Croatia. And now, please, allow me if I say that it could not be applied in the civil war that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me move on to another subject. Sir, on page 65 of the transcript, the first day you testified, which I guess was Tuesday, the 5th of February, you were -- let me get the quote for you, sir, what you stated so that I don't misquote it. Sorry, I have the wrong day. I have the wrong transcript in my hand. It's the 3rd of February. It's the first day, as I stated, but the 3rd of February. And beginning on line 1, you stated: "Not only in the area of Kozarac, but there were also barricades in villages so to say. The people organised themselves, they put up defence - and I'm sorry but that transcript is missing a word - and suggestions came from the Crisis Staff for the obstacles could be removed so the traffic could start moving freely. And in most cases, it bore fruit, but in this case it was fruitless." Sir, where do you hear of these suggestions from the Crisis Staff for the removal of obstacles?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to illustrate this by confirming that there were barricade, that there were obstacles even at places where this was not necessary. It happened to me when I was travelling from Tuzla that I was stopped by uniformed guys. They searched my car, and they took quite a lot of things from the car. Later on, I read in the press that they were rogue policemen who were looting in that area. The reaction was that people organised themselves in certain areas and certain villages. I believe that I have already said it, as tensions increased, and everybody was afraid, people were afraid. And I heard on Radio Prijedor and on television the thing that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us, you used the word "suggestions" from the Crisis Staff. On these radio and television announcements, did they say the Crisis Staff suggests to people that they remove the barricades? Did they use that word, or did they use a stronger word?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I may have used the wrong term. I can't remember the very wording, but I think it may even have been an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on page 56 of the same day's transcript, you talked about an incident that happened -- let me read your entire answer to try to put it into context beginning on line 9. You were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Were you ever present at the handover of any weapons?" And you answered: "It happened a little before these fatal events in Prijedor. It was sometime between the 15th and 20th of May. I can't be more precise than that. I went to see the secretary for agriculture in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, Mr. Ranko Travar. And on my way in, I met an acquaintance from Cereci - I may be mispronouncing it. Those times -- and it was a long time ago, so I can't remember his name. And he was seeking to extend the deadline for the return of weapons. And I heard them talking about this in the entrance because they hadn't managed to complete that part of the job." Sir, the gentleman from Cereci - and you can correct my pronunciation if I'm mispronouncing that - who was he speaking to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I will correct you in two respects. First of all, I went to see the secretary for the economy. And secondly, the name of the village is Cereci. I know that it may be difficult to pronounce. One detail that really struck in my memory was that the man was quite frightened, and he was seeking extension for the deadline for the turnover of weapons. I think I said after that that there were soldiers standing in the immediate vicinity. I couldn't tell who exactly he was addressing in order to seek extension. I think he was asking for two hours more. Part of the weapons, he said as he was passing by, had already been returned. That's what was said, but I can't tell who he was seeking extension from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just so we're clear, when you say for the secretary for the economy, that was Mr. Travar's title at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this village, Cereci, is that located within the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very close to the town itself. I think it's even considered part of the town. I know this village quite well. It's a 60 per cent Muslim village, and then also Croatians and Serbs living there. A relative of mine was married there, and when these unfortunate events started happening, part of -- some of the people from that village were spending time at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where in the Municipal Assembly building did you overhear this conversation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it was on yesterday's transcript, I have page 54, line 5, you were discussing the fact that some of the equipment from the Ljubija mine was mobilised, and for that equipment, you received a list, some paper. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. This document was actually a mobilisation list. It's an army document, the army sends the document certifying that the army had taken possession of something and that it hadn't been stolen so you knew where it was. So in case the equipment was destroyed during the war, there would be damages paid for these equipments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that the Omarska facility was taken over by force by the military and police. Did you receive any such paper regarding the mobilisation of all of the equipment of the mine that you were responsible for as the chief officer of the company, that the army had taken over?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite accurate, in the first phase, I got such certificates for all the mobile equipment that had been engaged by the army. But I did not receive any document after the facilities at Omarska were taken over. Then it happened in the late 1995 and early 1996. They offered a contract for the army to come in with their people and stay there in the facilities in order to set up their own barracks there. I never signed this contract. I never agreed with them, but completely irregardless of that, and in spite of the fact that I never signed an agreement with them, they came in and occupied the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm concentrating -- I'll try to concentrate this morning on 1992. Sir, in 1992, after the camp investigation centre - whatever you want to call it - in Omarska was set up, you indicated that was in late May. For the period between that and when the foreign journalists visited Omarska, which to remind you was August the 5th, I believe, but just to be clear, let's take the months of June and July. For those two months, June and July of 1992, did the Ljubija mines continue to have on its payroll those employees of the mine at Omarska who were working at the camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday when we watched the tape, I said that we had managed to get funds from Smederevo and from a department store in Banja Luka to pay the people their salaries. But after that, the workers of none of the three ethnic backgrounds received any further salary simply because there were no funds to pay the salaries from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were people such as electricians at the Omarska mine of Serbian ethnicity, did they remain on the payroll -- whether they received their salary or not, did they remain on the payroll of the Ljubija mine company while working at the camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to find the right words to provide you with an adequate answer. What I can tell you is that no one selected payrolls at that time. And please remind me, I said that in 1993, I did sign dismissals so that we could have a definite situation concerning the work force at the iron ore mine. The president of the Executive Board asked for these lists, but I wouldn't give them to him. It was a secret the company had to keep. It was a secret document. So they were all on these lists but no salaries were paid at that time. It was only at a later stage in 1994 when we got some funding from Smederevo, we paid the salary again. And then there was an embargo imposed on Republika Srpska, and even that stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on to a different subject, and that is you were discussing yesterday with Mr. Lukic the removal of Dr. Stakic from the position of president of the Municipal Assembly, and that movement that began in late 1992 led to his removal in early 1993. You said beginning on page 9, the top line: "I did know some of these people. They were members of the SDS, and there was a belligerent group, a belligerent faction there, a group of people who were -- were not happy with the assembly's work up to that point. They weren't happy with the way Dr. Stakic led the assembly, chaired the assembly. Dusan Kurnoga was among those people." In fact, sir, Mr. Kurnoga is the person who replaced Dr. Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Not only Kurnoga, Mandic came to the head of the Executive Board also. I think his name was Dusan Mandic, but I may be wrong about this. Dusan Mandic. These people were very dismissive to people who had occupied positions before the war. In addition to Kurnoga, there was Zmijanac, there was a man named Sidjak. I explained before that he had been appointed the director of Energopetrol company. He had embezzled 450.000 German marks and ended up in prison. And later on, in 1994 and 1995, because of this Tribunal, there was an intervention from the top of the state, from the top level of the leadership of the state for the whole thing to stop. And that was when Dr. Stakic was again appointed as the president. Please, I'm not sure I can remember exactly the time frame, but I think that was in 1996 that he again became president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say the top level of the republic, the president of the SDS party at that time was Dr. Karadzic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me, during the time that Mr. Kurnoga was president of the Municipal Assembly, having replaced Dr. Stakic, did any camps such as Omarska or Keraterm or anything the equivalent to Omarska and Keraterm exist when Mr. Kurnoga was the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. Of course, a period followed in which fronts were set up, so there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know Dr. Stakic? You've mentioned a few occasions, but can you tell us how well you know him and in what way you know Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the best way to get to know someone, to familiarise yourself with someone, is in informal moments. We used to play cards together as I have mentioned. And at a later stage, we started shooting pool together. And his and my wife when we were away, we would have a drink or two also. And we used to talk about everything, all kinds of things. I remember that in late 1995 or early 1996, I told him that he should take an MA, and he was a young man. He had a wonderful wife and children. So I thought it would have been a good idea for him to enroll in an MA programme. That's what I told him, and I know that he did so later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In social sessions, you talked about shooting pool and playing cards -- or playing billiards and playing cards, did Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Drljaca also socialise with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period that I was spending time with Dr. Stakic, I must say there were only three restaurants working in Prijedor. They had priority because there was a shortage of electricity. But those three restaurants did get electricity. So most of us would come together there. I would meet Dr. Stakic. Dr. Kovacevic never played pool. And Simo Drljaca was always surrounded literally by his escort, and literally I had no possibility to come even close to him. And I don't think Dr. Stakic did either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So at these few open restaurants such as Kotpolje, you would see Mr. Kovacevic who would observe the pool games but not play, billiard games, and you would also see Mr. Drljaca, but you didn't socialise directly with him yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I didn't. If it happened that we were standing close to each other, it was only because different players were taking over at the pool table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in these conversations, social conversations you had with Dr. Stakic at the time you saw him in the basement of the Municipal Assembly, you said, doing the night shift for the Crisis Staff, did you ever talk to him about what you had described I believe on page 72 of yesterday's transcript, when I asked you about certain colleagues of yours, directors of the Ljubija mine and then prominent persons in Prijedor such as Mr. Seric, Dr. Sadikovic, Mr. Cehajic, you said that, beginning on line 10: "After those events, news arrived but from the street. Certain names were mentioned. They said that those persons had been killed." Did you ever talk about these rumours to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, not at all. I did not discuss those rumours with anyone at all. Simply because I refused to believe that any such thing was true. And I'll give you another name, Mr. Softic, he was an optician in Prijedor. He was a marriage witness of a friend of mine, so I learned about his arrest. But later on, I realised that he returned from the camp and went to Split and that all his equipment was returned to him. That's one of the reasons I refused to participate in spreading these rumours which, as I said yesterday -- unfortunately those colleagues of mine that you refer to yesterday, those people are now gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic in these conversations with you ever discuss the disappearance or killing of persons he knew of these prominent persons or other persons or the destruction of places like Kozarac, Stari Grad, the main churches and mosques in Prijedor? Did Dr. Stakic talk to you about those?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must point out that I only came twice when Dr. Stakic was on duty. And again, we didn't discuss any of these subjects. We were playing cards or chess, so sometimes if the phone rang, he would give instruction to the utility services of the town. But we didn't discuss any such things at all, and this does not only apply to Dr. Stakic; I did not discuss these subjects with any of the people who were on duty. I came maybe two, three, or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Aside from these times in the Municipal Assembly, the other times that you did not discuss these things with Dr. Stakic was when you saw him at restaurants, playing cards, playing billiards, sharing a drink?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my deepest conviction, and I'm speaking for myself, but I had the same impression about him and a couple of other colleagues. We were trying to escape from that reality. I was looking for a space where I could get a reprieve, not have to think about it. Not to double-check these rumours. Perhaps I was seeking to convince myself that those rumours were not true. And that was the chief reason why -- at least for myself I tried to avoid the subjects. But I think the same is true for Dr. Stakic; we simply tried to avoid these subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic. I have some questions for you. You first told us about an incident of a family in Zagreb that you read in the press at that moment. You afterwards yesterday, I think, told us that you were not used to read Kozarski Vjesnik - I can't say the name, sorry - because it was not a reliable newspaper or at least a weekly publication. You told us also that there was a journalist that had been related to the iron ore mine that afterwards went to work to this paper and was the one who gave you a copy of the announcement of the takeover. Can you just be a little more precise what were the newspapers you were reading at the time and what was this relationship with this journalist? Because I remember some very hard comments you made about the journalist on this other newspaper. Can you precise this for us.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can specify, Your Honour. I find I must say that this is a local newspaper, Kozarski Vjesnik. I did not read Kozarski Vjesnik because I did not consider their journalists to represent any high professional standards of their trade. I received a copy of the announcement from Mr. Rajlic on the 30th. It is true that he had worked at the iron ore mine previously, and later he went to Kozarski Vjesnik. He worked for Kozarski Vjesnik for a while, and I think after all the events, he was appointed a secretary to the embassy in the Vatican. The other news that I could follow was on TV Zagreb because after the transmitter on Mount Kozara had been taken, we could no longer watch TV Sarajevo. The only thing we could watch was TV Banja Luka, and partly TV Belgrade. I directed my own transmitter to TV Zagreb, and the newspaper I was reading during that period was Politika, a daily paper from Belgrade. It was from those media that I found out about the Zec family, and I was interested in the case because I think they came from Dragotija. I'm not entirely sure but I think they were from Dragotija, which is a village about 20 kilometres from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think that Mr. Rajlic - I'm sorry for the pronunciation - was a reliable journalist?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can judge that. But after all, he was appointed a secretary at the embassy in the Vatican. They must have checked his credentials, his work, and all his other personal information. If he managed to pass that particular test, perhaps that might lead me to conclude that he was, after all, an honest man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You're not so sure. Sorry. That's a side comment. Then you told us a lot about the iron mine, iron ore mine, but I'm not very clear about the times. You said that usually in spring or summer each year, you had not a lot of work, so it was usual for the company to have a lot of employees on pay leave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think there has been a misunderstanding. I'm going to try to explain this at least in as far as I can. The Ljubija iron ore mine is the biggest producer of iron ore in the former Yugoslavia. We produced 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, I had understood that. I only wanted precise some times because it's very confusing for us in terms of the split of the company because of a decision of some employees or some group of employees. And then afterwards you said that the production has already stopped because of the war and all that. So I want to just precise the times. If I have to understand you correctly, if you say that the production has stopped because of the war, that means the war in Croatia or Slovenia that was in 1991. So I suppose that the mine was not functioning in 1992. Can you clarify these periods of time for us.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I appreciate that we only have limited time at our disposal, so I'm going to try to be as specific as I can. Until the very end of 1992, we worked full capacity. And the seasons, the different seasons, and the changing of the seasons didn't matter to our production. Our production was not affected. At the beginning of 1992, the work of the banks and the lines of transactions were being disrupted across the territory of the former Yugoslavia, but we couldn't get the due payments to come from in Italy even. So at the end of March, we stopped our operation and our depots were full. The ore was being shipped to Zenica and to Smederevo all the time, not to the west because in Croatia there weren't any significant iron ore mines with the exception of Sisak was not a very good iron ore mine. So until the end of 1991, we worked to full capacity, full throttle, so you're clear about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had already stopped operations by the end of March. So Omarska as a mine was not operating in May. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of April, many of our workers were on paid leave which means previously we had shifts of 200 or 300 people. Now some of those people were kept because some of those people were at home, but some of those people were needed at the iron ore mine for maintenance and reparation work in order to keep watch over such equipment as needed to be maintained and repaired all the time to prevent flooding in the mines. I can't give you the exact number of workers who were still there, but I will tell you that the production line, production floor, different production floors at iron ore mines had their own directors, but then those were coordinators and they answered to me. But I didn't go down to the field to check for myself, and I can't give you the exact numbers of people who were on paid leave at the time or those people who were there working. I only had the lists, the pay lists, delivered to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'm clear about that. You said it three or four times already. But also you mentioned the person who was in charge, and I don't dare pronounce the name, but that you were always having news from the Omarska camp as the takeover from the military not directly from the one who was the head at that place, and you told us who, but by other means. What happened to this gentleman that he never communicated with you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point I said that I stayed at home for a few days. I didn't leave the house. I was looking after my family and after my sons. I suppose that the director in question did the same. I cannot pinpoint where he was during that period of time. I believe that you have enough information to tell you that I went to the Security Services Centre to get a certificate, passes, and from that you can see where people were at the time. I can't tell you where this particular gentleman was at that time. I would call it a black hole in the information at that time. I'm talking about the period in late May up to the 5th or 6th of June. It was very difficult to know at the time where people were, so I can't really tell you where that gentleman was during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You were not surprised that he didn't inform you of the takeover of the mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't inform me during that period of time. It was only later on that I learned that this was turned into an investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Some moments ago, you said that you stayed at home for a few days, and you said that also yesterday. I remember that, or the day before yesterday. What was this period of time that you stayed at home? You said a few days. Which period?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I really can't tell you whether it was four, five, or six days. But in any case, it was in the period from the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May and later on, further on after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I was asking. And then you told us yesterday, and I would like to mention the line, but I have the LiveNote, and they are not very clear. But you told us that you wore a uniform for around five or ten days after the end of May, and I remember Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the videotape that was shown yesterday, you were wearing a uniform, and it was on the 20th of June. So that means more than five or ten days again -- it's okay, but I can't find it. Why were you wearing a uniform if you were staying at home?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I stayed at home for a few days, and I told you during which period that was. I did wear the uniform for a bit longer. I can't tell you exactly when it was exactly. I'm sure that I wore the uniform up to the end of June. Now I can tell you more precisely because I have been faced with some documents. And with that videotape, I couldn't tell you precisely yesterday. But yes, I did wear the uniform for a longer period of time, up to the end of June probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But you didn't answer why. My question was: Why were you wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For personal safety and I wore a uniform and I carried a pistol, a short-barrelled pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You told us also that you were going to play cards or chess with the persons in the Crisis Staff who were having night duties or something like that. And you told us that you went around 9.00 and stayed until 12.00 by night. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. And if you will allow me, I would like to correct you. We played cards. We didn't play chess, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Doesn't matter. You had a special pass to be out at 12.00 by night? Because if I remember correct, there was a curfew from 10.00 by night? And if you were out at 12.00 by night, were you having -- did you have a special pass to be out during the curfew hours?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the initial stages, I did have a time-barred pass. I can't give you the exact date, whether it was for a period of two or three days. But every time when I went home, I used Mr. Sidjak's car. Mr. Sidjak was there, as I've told you. And he would give me a lift also for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: This morning, in line 7 of page 7, you told us that you were not sure about the reimbursement arrangements of the military during 1992. But I remember that you were shown the list of employees by the Defence counsel, and you identified a lot of them on military duty. So by the document you were shown today, you should pay or have in your payroll the employees who were doing military duty. The company was entitled to reimbursement by the military because of mobilisation. Why were you not aware of what the situation of reimbursement was? It was one of your duties as a manager, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lists of employees which were militarily engaged I took to Banja Luka. This was not done in the Prijedor garrison because it's a small garrison. It was done in the centre whose name I don't know. I believe it was the military command of Krajina. That is where I look the lists to a colonel whose name I have forgotten. And we were never reimbursed for the salaries that we paid out to the employees of the mine who were militarily engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll turn to another subject, please. In the transcript of I think it's Monday, Monday, 3 February, and I have the number of the pages, 11.658. I don't know if that's correct. In line 8 of this transcript, 7 and 8, you said -- you started some lines before: "Through my secretary, I informed the production floors in Omarska..." Et cetera, et cetera. "In the central workshop and the others that we already identified, I informed all of them that there had been a takeover by the SDS and that they should continue working normally." Then yesterday, you told us that the takeover was staged by the military and the SDS followed suit. This is a contradiction with what you said on Monday. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised this in my yesterday's statement, and I said that it was my very personal view, very, very personal. This is what I believe regardless of what had been communicated at that time, and that was that the SDS had taken over power. It is my impression that those people were the military because they wore uniforms, because that's who I saw at 5.00 in the morning when I arrived at the mine, and that's what I said yesterday, that it was my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You saw soldiers in your company at 5.00 in the morning that day, soldiers that were sent to tell you that everything should go on normally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that they called me, but they had already been in the mine on the premises of the mine, and that's where they called me from. And I told you that I didn't know any of these people. I can't tell you whether the uniforms were military uniforms or police uniforms. I only know that they were all in uniforms, and that's when they told me that we should continue working normally. And I've already told you that this was in town, in the centre of the town where there are about 200 people working, so I had to work with all of them. I told them that we should continue working. And it is correct that I communicated via my secretary by phone, and I spoke to all of my directors of various production plants and various sectors. And I told them that they should continue working normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'll try to be a little more concrete because I suppose you're not understanding what I want you to tell me. You didn't know even if there were soldiers or police personnel who were at your company just telling you that everything should go on normally. So why are you supposing that the military were the ones who were staging this takeover that you first said was done by the SDS? Can you see the difference in what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your explanation is really fantastic. It is true that there is a difference in my statements, but let me once again emphasise that I have shared with you my very personal view, not a general view. And wherever I voiced that personal opinion of mine, whoever I said that personal opinion, they didn't believe me and they tried to prove me wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And move to another subject, if I may. Sorry, just a moment, please. In your testimony on Monday, and I've just lost the page again -- oh, here it is. On page 11.705, you said that "In the first part of June - that's line 20 - over 30 per cent of the work force of the mine were militarily engaged, a vast majority were at home on standby. During the month of June, I asked people to call in so that we could compile the lists. In later stages, over 90 per cent of the total work force of the mine were militarily engaged. The only persons remained working were women and myself." And that was the month of June 1992. Some moments ago, you told us that the work was going on as usual during all the year 1992. How is it possible?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one or two things. I never said that we continued working throughout 1992. I don't think I have. In 1992, we worked in January, in February, and after that, the production was interrupted. And I told you that at that time, about 30 per cent of the people were militarily engaged. I may have omitted to mention that in 1995, there were over 95 per cent of the work force militarily engaged, and that the only people that remained in the company at that time were women and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You told us, and I think this was on Tuesday, not on Monday, that you were informed that there was looting or robberies of equipment in the Omarska mine, and you mentioned the 6th Sana Brigade. And can you tell me, that was from the JNA, that brigade? To which army did the brigade form a part, this 6th Sana Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very -- it's going to be very difficult for me to explain that. I'm not that familiar with that particular matter, but I'll try. Brigades consisted of the reserve members of the force, and I believe that it was according to the regulations governing the JNA. I believe that's how it was possible to mobilise the reserve military and include them into those particular brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: That's not my question. I wanted to know if this 6th Sana Brigade was a part of the army, the Yugoslav army, whatever the name you want to give it.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I did say that they were mobilised according to the regulations governing the JNA. So I believe that it would ensue from that this brigade was in the composition of the JNA, but I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. You told us the 6th Sana Brigade was taking things from Omarska in the spring, summer, or autumn 1992. And you made a list of special tools like two sets of "zol" keys and all that sort of things. And you just put to several robberies of private character took place. If the Omarska complex was taken over by the military by the end of May, and that was spring of 1992, how can you make a difference between a private character or private nature of the robberies and just a mobilisation of equipment that you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really apologise. I didn't say that the 6th Sana Brigade was engaged in the looting in Omarska. I mentioned the central mines and eastern mines, that is in Tomasica. So this is a fact, and I can provide my comment. The lists have been compiled, and now it is being asked from the government of Republika Srpska to pay the damages. But they cannot do that given the economic situation as it is nowadays. But as for the investigation centre, I can't tell you exactly when this -- these premises were emptied, and then we did the stock of Omarska, and we could then tell when was it that the armed citizens of Omarska entered and took all sorts of tools. And based on that, we compiled a list of these things, and we handed them over to this public security centre. And I believe that I've already told you that nothing was done in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: When you got the news of the Omarska takeover by the military, couldn't you just lay a complaint on that with Mr. Ranko Travar who was the person in charge in the municipality? I mean in this field. I don't mean the president or the vice-president. He was in charge of this mining thing.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at that time, no complaint could have borne fruit, could have been seen through. This was a state in which civilians could not complain in any way about the actions of the army and the behaviour of the MUP. I may have complained orally; I can't remember at this point. But my personal opinion is that at that time, a human's life was not worth much. And in that chaos, one could not make a distinction between the regular army and others. There were also paramilitary units. I really did not see any doors on which I could knock and have my complaint listened to and seen through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Wasn't it your duty as a manager of the company just to put on paper, let's say write or advise your legal advisors, to take some action or lay a complaint or something?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal services were not functioning. And let me put it simply: At that moment, I did not have at my disposal any instruments, any tools, any means to prevent these things. And there was nobody for me to address and complain. Whatever I had done, things would not have changed. You may have been -- you may be right. Maybe I should have complained. Maybe I should have filed documents. I didn't. I'm a timid person by nature, and I was afraid myself. Maybe it is my fault that I was not more aggressive at that time. It is maybe my fault that I did not write documents, write letters. But to put it simply, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, on Monday, you stated, transcript page 32, starting with line 6: "In the morning on 30th of April, 1992, I was called -- I received a call at 5.00 in the morning, and I was told to come to the administrative building. They didn't tell me why I was supposed to go there. They just told me that it was urgent, and I went to the administrative building, and I found there some people in uniform." Can you tell us who telephoned you? Who told you to come to the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who telephoned introduced himself and told me that he was calling from the management building. I didn't remember, didn't retain that family name, the name of that person because I never saw him again. I obviously had to go because I was afraid that there may have been a disaster. And one tends to react instinctively when somebody calls you at 5.00 in the morning, I did not have the time. I just rushed to the headquarters, and that's where I saw the people in uniforms and that's when they told me what they told me. At first, when this guy called me, he didn't tell me what it was all about. He just told me that the thing was urgent, and I rushed to my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I believe that you were, and I hope you are, one of the most respected and influential persons in Prijedor Municipality and among the Prijedor establishment. And then somebody called you at 5.00 in the morning, and you immediately came -- obeyed to his order and came to the mine. How can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have security at the mines in all the production floors and at the management building, too. I can't know the names of all guards who were there. There were over 120 of them. So the person who called told me he was calling from the management headquarters. I just don't remember his name. I was afraid that something unexpected had happened at the mine, a disaster maybe, and that that's why I received a call from security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. My next question: Yesterday, you told us that late in May 1992, you were supplied with gun and uniform. May I ask you who supplied you with gun and uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We bought our uniforms using money from the budget of the mines. That means, the mines provided for the uniforms, and I was given the pistol by security. Excuse me, please, let me specify this: The security service of the mines itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. And one more question: Yesterday, you stated at transcript page 10, lines 2-4, "the SDS had power but no money, and that's why they decided to remove the 12 managing directors of the state-owned enterprises." Can you explain to me what is the connection between the powerful SDS and without money, and how this situation can be cured by removing the directors of the state-owned enterprises?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this particular group of people in the SDS identified, the group of Kurnoga, Zmijanac, Sidjak, and Mandic, they came to the conclusion, they came to the conclusion that they had power but no money. And they believed if they had their own people in place, appointed managing directors of the companies, the companies would have to pay money to them. That's a fact. In 1999, I received a request from the SNS party for 2.000 German marks to be paid into their account. So that was common practice then, but it still seems to be the way certain people go about their business even these days. And I paid this with my own dismissal. They removed from the position of the managing director of the Nemet company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask you, what was the car you drove in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I had a Commodore, that's the make, Commodore. And later, I got a Renault 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, did you drive this car throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not throughout 1992, not the whole time. I was also using a Golf, Playtrade's Golf. It's an export company in Prijedor. The car belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, whenever you needed fuel, did you refuel your car or your cars at Banja Luka Road, at the petrol station at Banja Luka Road?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the whole of 1991 and part of 1992, we filled our petrol at our own petrol stations in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So also your private-owned car or the car used by the Playtrade, they were refuelled in Ljubija? You always drove especially to Ljubija to refuel your car. Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did specify for the whole of 1991 and part of 1992, we were using the petrol we had within the perimeter of the central mines in Ljubija. After June and July, we no longer went there for petrol. I don't know exactly where our drivers were getting petrol, but they were certainly no longer using that particular petrol station within the perimeter of the Ljubija central mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be your testimony you never drove alone and refuelled your car; it was done by your drivers, correct? And you were never present, never, when the car was refuelled?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this particular interval while Mr. Faruk was the driver, he did it regularly. In mid-1992, I still went to Belgrade on my own to the Sartik company, and then I bought my fuel myself mostly in Belgrade or at petrol stations in Serbia because in the area of the corridor, there was no petrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many cars of the Prijedor ore mines company were still operational after the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Renault 25, the driver who was my driver kept the car. I know there was a Lada caravan, the delivery vehicle of the central workshop. And I know there was a Volkswagon caddy which had gauges, electrical gauges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about those cars you mentioned during your testimony several times, the huge lorries, for example, the TAMici?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are vehicles which kept in the production lines and in the central workshop. I will say again, the production lines, central mines, eastern mines, and Omarska mines. But the central workshop is in Prijedor. So all these vehicles starting with the heavy mining machines and dumpers to the TAM vehicles that we used to refer to as the TAMici, a tonne and a half or 2, they were freight lorries which could carry up to 20 tonnes. They were in the auto service where the buses were, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These lorries ever leave the compound of, say, Ljubija mines or Omarska? I'm always referring only to the period of time May through September 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to give you an accurate answer to that question. All the freight vehicles -- none of the freight vehicles were registered for public transportation, for public traffic. The vehicles which could carry up to 20 tonnes were registered for public traffic, but these heavy freight vehicles used to transport goods by road were mostly kept at the Autoservice. I can't tell you if these vehicles, and when, commuted between the central mines and the central workshop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true that especially the TAMici had ordinary car plates, and having these plates, they could drive also on public roads?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As I said, they were registered for public roads. All the vehicles of the mines were registered for public roads with the exception of the heavy machines like dumpers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the question would be: Did you know where these cars when, for instance, leaving the areas of the one or other mines were ever refuelled in Prijedor? Did you ever need a certificate by the Crisis Staff for getting fuel?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. We did not get fuel in that way. All our vehicles in the Omarska mines had their own petrol stations in Omarska. And vehicles kept in Prijedor would get their petrol in Ljubija where there was also a petrol station. I'm talking about both oil and petrol. In Omarska, I think they only had oil tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with your driver the question whether or not for your own car or cars you needed such a certificate from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He never told me anything about any such thing, nor was I aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever read the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was -- it wasn't being delivered to me. We were subscribed to the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you were never informed about that what would be important for your company, orders, recommendations issued by in previous time the Municipal Assembly or later the Crisis Staff? You were not interested at all in this?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to explain this. All correspondence with the Executive Board from the municipality and the bodies of power, government, in municipality went directly across in writing. In mid-1992, the municipality wanted to engage part of the machinery we had, and that was approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Document S180, item number 24. Just in order of the limited time, let me direct you to number 2, last dash, "the following may sign refuelling orders: For the Crisis Staff vehicles, secretary of the municipal secretariat for the economy and social affairs." That would be which person, the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the secretariat for the economy, I think Ranko Travar was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Travar - apparently you met him several times - that he had to follow this order as we can read it here in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss this with him. I mentioned upon leaving for Slavonia, and several times later I did see him, but we didn't discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a shortage of fuel in May, June, July, August, September in Prijedor? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the action taken in order to distribute the fuel in an adequate way?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is your testimony that you don't know about certificates issued by the Crisis Staff on -- or granting petrol or oil to certain persons?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was born very near Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know a building in Cirkin Polje where those certificates were issued?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the building in a manner of speaking because I once was in the building. If I remember correctly, a man from Cirkin Polje, I think his last name is Makovac asked to have part of the resources of the mines put at his disposal, his disposal personally. I refused his request, and I never went back to that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall by chance the road and number where this building was located?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The street is called Bolnicka Street, the hospital street. But I can't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I once again ask, you lived in what area and explicitly the street and number, the street where you lived at that time, the middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Dzemala Bijedica Street, number 14/6. And I still reside in the same flat, but the street name has been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming back to this building, when entering this building, did you see any insignia or any name related to those being in power now or even the name "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember at all. I arrived there in a vehicle, and I wasn't really paying attention. There must have been some kind of staff there, if I remember the way Mr. Makovac was behaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you receive a new ID at the end of April 1992 or beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've had to change so many different IDs that I can no longer remember. I suppose this may have been the case. If we had new registration plates issued, I suppose they issued us with new IDs, too. I can't remember specifically, believe me. But if that was done, then I must have been issued a new ID at some point, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This ID would have been issued by whom?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: IDs are issued by the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wasn't it an alternative that the -- an ID was issued in this same building in Cirkin Polje? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite concrete, the ID was issued by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the question put to you by Judge Vassylenko, was it a special ID allowing you to remain on the streets of Prijedor during curfew?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was such an ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What other special privileges were combined with this ID?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a pass which gave you the right to move about during curfew. It was not an ID proper. It was just a document, a pass, making it possible for you to move about during curfew. And I was not aware of any other privileges related to that pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your final testimony that you never entered this building in Cirkin Polje being you yourself or waiting in the car, that your driver did it, asking for any certificate to get fuel. And it's in addition your testimony, and question mark should be read on the transcript, that you never refuelled or your driver did never refuel in your presence the car or one of the cars at Banja Luka Road petrol station or, I add now, Zarko Zrenjanin barracks?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was once at the building in the Bolnicka Street, the building you just referred to, but only once. I think it was the beginning of May. That was my submission. As far as the refuelling of the vehicle that I was using, the driver took care of that on a regular basis. So to the best of my knowledge, I can't claim that he didn't, but at least I was not aware of any such situations as you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher now to show from the same document S180, item 29. It's on page number 42, at least in English. Maybe this may appear repetitive. But it's related to the question whether or not, and if so, how, you received orders from the Crisis Staff. Have a look on this and please comment. It reads: "Ljubija RZR is hereby ordered to prohibit further supply of fuel for the purposes of the Omarska regional staff." Are you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss this order with Ranko Travar?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss this order with anyone because I was not aware of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Ranko Travar discuss this question with you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Turn to point 3: "Ranko Travar is hereby tasked with making arrangements with the Ljubija iron ore mines canteen for the provision of food for soldiers and members of the police force." Did you discuss this with Ranko Travar?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss this. Perhaps Ranko Travar had talked to the managing director of -- in charge of food for the staff of the iron ore mine. The managing director of what we refer to as the meals unit was Mandjlo Marcetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that you were not aware that the company you headed was ordered to supply with fuel and provide food for soldiers and members of the police. Is this your testimony, that you are not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again: I'm talking about number 1. The managing director Dusko Vlacina was at the head of Omarska. They may have talked to him, but they certainly didn't talk to me. The meals unit in this particular period was not formally part of the Ljubija iron ore mines. It was separated from the structure of the iron ore mines itself officially at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We learned during the testimony that the premises and the areas of your responsibility were spread all over - I don't know whether limited to - but spread all over the municipality of Prijedor. May I ask, how often between, say, 1990 and 1996 did you visit Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, not many times. I can't remember exactly. But I don't believe I was there for more than three or four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not for me to comment on this, but maybe you can understand that one is surprised to hear that you, as the head of all these institutions, mines, and so on - you mentioned all the details already - that you rather randomly visited the one or other mine or institution. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, to come immediately to the point, could you please repeat when had you been the last time before May 1992 in Omarska ore mine and when was it the next time you had been there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when I was in Omarska. I was sometime in the course of 1991, that's for sure. And I'm also sure that after March 1992, I was not in Omarska again until sometime in 1995 or 1996. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you were not interested in at all what was happening in Omarska in your own company during the entire year 1992? You were not present one only day, one only hour, absolutely no visit to Omarska mine? Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you try to land with the Piper aircraft at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was during the construction phase in the 1980s when the grounds were laid for the pista. So that's when I couldn't land because of the lighting columns that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this attempt to land had nothing to do with the actual construction and the actual buildings in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I flew a Super K Piper, a two-seater, and with me was the guy who was the -- guy who sold us the equipment. So he wanted to see the whole compound of Omarska from the air. And at that point, I thought maybe it would be good for us to land there. We didn't succeed, and we had to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, who was the owner of this aircraft?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Partizan Aviation Air Club from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's turn to another subject that was already covered several times during your testimony. You mentioned the 5th of February, Day 114, page 50; and today's transcript, page 31, line 10, when asked "Did you wear a uniform in 1992?" Your answer: "In late May of 1992 for the first 10 or 15 days." Today, you corrected your testimony up to the end of June. Why was it that the 5th of May [sic], you clearly remembered the first 10 or 15 days?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The 5th of May [sic], you testified you wore a uniform the first 10 or 15 days. Let me quote it in context. You were asked: "Sir, did you wear a uniform in 1992?" Answer: "In late May of 1992, for the first 10 or 15 days." Today, you testified "to the end of June." 31:10 of today's transcript. Why did you tell us the 5th of February, "late May for the first 10 or 15 days"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I based my testimony on my recollection, but it is very difficult to be precise after such a long period of time. And I even said that that may have been the end of June. I may have worn the uniform even after the end of June. It's very difficult for me to be absolutely accurate about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You already told us this morning that you bought the uniform, and you received a BT short-barrel rifle. The 5th of May [sic], you added Zastava, the name of this rifle. So who ordered you to wear both uniform and rifle?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not carry a rifle. I carried a pistol, a TT short-barrelled pistol. And it's nickname is TT. And it was made by Zastava. I can't tell you whether an order had been issued or not, but I'm sure that the driver and me and some other people wore uniforms for our own personal safety. We wanted to be different from other citizens. That's why we decided to put on uniforms, for personal safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The 5th of February, on page 91, you referred to a recent conversation with Mr. Dragic. When was this conversation? Page 91, line 8, 9.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 or 20 days ago approximately. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Had at that point in time Mr. Dragic already Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. testified before this Tribunal? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He had testified already?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him the issues discussed in the hearing Prosecutor versus Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of my company, I went to secure a loan. We spent a very short time together. He told me that he had testified. I know that he was in the secretariat. And then he told me about the problems with the setting up of the government, and he told me then that they had reached a stalemate position and they couldn't agree on the number of people who would be appointed to a certain number of positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss the question of uniforms with him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite concrete, how would it be that out of the blue, you decide to wear a uniform and then try to tell us it's for your own protection? I can understand that today, you testified you wore a rifle -- a pistol. On page 50 of the transcript on the 5th of February, it was translated, maybe once again it was once again a question of translation, but in any event, BT short-barrel rifle, Zastava was the make of the rifle. This was your testimony at this time. "This may serve for security purposes." But why for security purposes out of the blue wearing a uniform? Who ordered you to wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that there may have been an order. I really don't remember whether there was and who issued it. But personally, I believe that a uniform makes me different from the civilians, that it distinguished me from the civilians, and that I had the right to protection after the events that had taken place in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you regarded yourself no longer as a civilian. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not engaged in any military unit, so I was not a soldier. But I did have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which kind of uniform was it? JNA uniform? Camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform which was purchased in Celinac near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Including any insignia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
