utterances.text: Testimony, 5th of February, LiveNote Day 114, line 91: When answered on the question of -- about the question of legality of the president of the Municipal Assembly, you answered: "There was a previous agreement on who would be appointed the president of the Municipal Assembly, who would be appointed the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, and then after that, there was a long discussion between the parties on the distribution of various sectors and the executive branch of the government." You told us there was a previous agreement. Could you please explain us what was this previous agreement you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have chosen a wrong term. But it was the SDA which won a certain number of seats, more than any other parties. And then there was an interparty discussion at which it was agreed that the SDA would be given, awarded, the post of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and SDS would be awarded the post of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. Well, this was decided before the Municipal Assembly was set up, and then the Municipal Assembly, when it was set up, it was discussed who would actually the people be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sir, the question was, on page 90: "The assembly elected Muhamed Cehajic as the president and never elected Dr. Stakic, is it correct, as the president of the Municipal Assembly?" Your answer: "Again, you've put me in an awkward position. I've told you the Municipal Assembly was in session after the multiparty election." And then you continued: "There was a previous agreement on who would be appointed the president of the Municipal Assembly, who would be appointed the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly." Do you regard Dr. Stakic as the legal or the illegal president of the Municipal Assembly as from the takeover?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you regard the census of 1992 as an illegal or a legal one?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you allow me to say a few words about the census which took place in 1991 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to answer the question with a clear yes or no. You touched already upon this during yesterday's testimony. I apologise that I don't have the correct page with me. But therefore, once again, yes or no, do you regard this a legal or illegal or even to go one step further, a legitimate census?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really confused. I don't know whether you're asking me about the 1991 census, whether it was legal or illegal, or whether you're asking me about the appointment of Mr. Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly and whether you're asking me whether that appointment was legal or illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's severe the both questions. First question, please answer with yes or no, following the elections and then the takeover, did you regard Dr. Stakic as from the takeover as the legal president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you regard the census of 1991 legal or illegal? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you accept the outcome of this census?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accepted at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Dr. Stakic in the beginning of 1992 what one could do in order to rearrange the situation following the outcome of this census and later on the elections? Did you ever discuss these political problems with Dr. Stakic at that time where the -- there was not yet the crisis situation you mentioned later where you told us that from your point of view it would be better not to discuss political issues? But I want to refer to the period of the beginning of 1992. Did you ever discuss with Dr. Stakic the outcome of the census and later the outcome of the elections?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never discussed that. I didn't even know which party he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So were you aware that there were meetings in order to, to put it very carefully, to rearrange the situation in Prijedor starting with January 1992 aiming at having another government, once again to be neutral, another government in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk about that. Such documents were not available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't ask about documents. What documents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've mentioned meetings. So I meant documents from any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about such meetings when you yourself conclude that there would be some documents about these meetings, for example, minutes?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that minutes were taken. In 1992, I saw the minutes of the Executive Board of the SDA where some things were defined. So by way of analogy, I assume that the SDS also took minutes of their meetings, if there were meetings. But that's just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you hear for the first time about the takeover? Is it your testimony that it was at 5.00 the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No rumours, no discussions with friends beforehand?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the documents, first document presented by the Defence, this was the transcript of that what was read out during the entire day of the 30th of April from Radio Prijedor, that you received this document on or about 11.00 to 12.00 this same day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you receive this document spontaneously or did you request this document from the journalist?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many other similar documents you received spontaneously from this journalist?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any other documents from the journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The 3rd of February, 2003, day 112, page 60, you were asked about the duties of the Crisis Staff, meetings, and your answer was: "Yes, on two or three occasions, these were nighttime stints of duty. You would have to be on duty all night. And the office was on the basement next to the centre for early warning centre, and there were communications." And then it doesn't continue. Therefore, first question: This was in the municipal building or in another building? Because here you can't read the basement of which building? It only reads "in the basement next to the centre."

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the basement of the building of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then you continue: "It was there when Slavko Budimir was on duty, Ranko Travar, Mr. Milomir Stakic, and Sidjak was also with us. I don't know what his first name was, but he was not a member of the Crisis Staff." How do you know that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he drove me home in the night, like I've told you he did, he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I can't understand this. You're sitting together in a car, and a person tell us you: "I'm not a member of the Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were talking about the reasons for him being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who were so the other members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there a couple of times. I think I've given you four names, Mr. Milomir Stakic, Mr. Budimir, Mr. Travar, and Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Mr. Savanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about him. He may have been on duty, but at some point when I wasn't there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Macura?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To conclude my questions, you were the head of the most important industrial complex in the municipality of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You heard rumours about killings, rumours about persons missing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You had meetings together with Dr. Stakic and others you identified as members of the Crisis Staff, and you never took the opportunity to discuss these rumours with these persons?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you make any attempt to verify the rumours being in this position, having this special pass allowing you even at nighttimes to travel around? Didn't you take the opportunity to verify that these rumours were wrong by, for example, going to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made no such attempts. After my conversation with Simo Drljaca, when he told me that I should go instead of Matanovic, it was clear to me that there was no point in trying anything. So the answer is no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was a member of the management of the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the hierarchy in Omarska mine of the remaining staff members, employees in Omarska following the takeover of Omarska ore mine as such at the end of May 1992? Who was the head of the management?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Vlacina was at the head of the management. He has a degree in mining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Next in line would be? Was he directly -- or the other way around. Mirko Babic was directly subordinate to Dusko Vlacina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met him at the airport on my way here just in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever hear shooting in Prijedor at home, when being at home?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, when the town was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you hear ever shooting from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to conclude, it's your testimony that you never tried to find out yourself what, in fact, happened in this part of your enterprise, the Omarska previously iron ore mine, later used as a camp? You never tried to realise what happened there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was told, I had information, that it had become an investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it is your testimony that you discussed this never, never with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Judges conferred during the break, and there are no further questions at this moment from the side of the Bench. So therefore, it would be now for the Defence, if any questions on the basis -- for the purpose of the re-examination. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have a few questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good afternoon, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just briefly return to a number of questions asked by the Honourable Chamber or my colleagues from the Prosecution. We want to shed light on a number of issues. You explained to us that the iron ore mine Ljubija was a very complex company consisting of a number of companies. The companies that -- the subcompanies that were part of the company of the iron ore mine Ljubija at large, did each of these subcompanies have their own managing director?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Each had their own managing director.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did each of these subcompanies that were part of the larger structure have their own administrative structure?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had all the structures of administration aside from the finances unit, the financial unit and the bookkeeping, the accountancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 89, line 2 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution asked you the following question: "How is it possible that someone who is the boss of everyone in Prijedor Municipality is made to stand duty by the telephone and night duty, that nighttime duty?" The president of the Municipal Assembly, was he boss to anyone at the Municipal Assembly? Was he boss to any of the employees of the Municipal Assembly, any of the members of the Executive Board or any of the assistance services?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't boss to any of those. He was, as I said, elected by the assembly, and he presided over the assembly. The subject matter debated at the assembly is prepared by the Executive Board and the secretariat. And then these materials are processed by technical services, technical services which is under the authority of the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, who is also elected at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 95, line 4, the Prosecution asked the following question: "Had the announcement been prepared prior to the 30th of April, 1992?" Tell us if you remember - if you don't remember, we can show you the document again - in the announcement, is there any reference to the date 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the date of the 29th of April, 1992, was referred to in the context of the ministry at the Bosnia and Herzegovina level whose head was Mr. Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that it would not have been possible to prepare this announcement before the afternoon or the evening of the 29th of April, or for that matter, during the morning of the 30th of April, 1992, at least not the announcement that we have been looking at the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer your question. It's only by analogy that I can attempt to answer this question. If the date, the 20th [as interpreted] of April was referred to, then this leads me to conclude that the text was drafted after the 29th of April. But I can only state this by analogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, Your Honours, page 54, line 16, it says "20th of April" was referred to, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt it should refer to 29th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher be so kind and show the witness Exhibit S77, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please, at the same time, if any, the English translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conclusion of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality speaks about the possibilities of establishing criteria on the mode of payment of paying salaries to the army and the police. The companies at that time, were they paying salaries, in as far as there were any at all, to people who had been mobilised by the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about the Ljubija iron ore mine company. No, the salaries of our people who had been mobilised by the police or the army were not being paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if those same people were receiving salaries from the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are done with this document. Could the usher please show the witness the Exhibit Number S308, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, would you be so kind, please, and read out the entire item 4 in this document.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For employees registered as missing persons or prisoners, the calculation and payment of salaries will be effected based on the actual working hours in May with the balance up to a full salary calculated and paid as if they had been on standby."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please continue.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Employees serving in the military and police units will not receive their salaries from the cashier unless they produce a certificate issued either by the competent military command (Zarko Zrenjanin barracks) or the Prijedor public security station. "The managers of enterprises, organisations, and sociopolitical communities are bound by this conclusion to penalize any failure to respond to the work obligation by dismissing such employees from work. "This conclusion shall become effective immediately. The SDK public auditing service of Prijedor and the managers of enterprises, organisations, and communities will be in charge of its implementation. "President, Dr. Milomir Stakic. "Submit to all enterprises, organisations, and sociopolitical communities, the SDK of Prijedor and the secretary for information."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, is it your testimony that in addition to a decision by the Crisis Staff that salaries were to be paid despite the lack of money, no salaries were paid and there were no salaries being paid to anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no salaries were being paid because there were huge problems with the cash flow, and the iron ore mine of Ljubija was short of money anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last article of this document says that "All employees failing to respond to the work obligation should be dismissed." Did this apply to everyone, or is it clear on the basis of this decision that there had been some form of discrimination related to a person's ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this decision was taken from the law -- the labour law, and the labour law envisages exactly when a dismissal can ensue; that's if a person fails to report for work for five days or longer. And this applies to all employees, at least as far as the employees of the iron ore mine of Ljubija are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 19, line 15 of today's transcript, one spoke about the announcement published by the Crisis Staff. You said that perhaps the word "order" had even been used. This was in relation to checkpoints. This public announcement or public address, did this apply to everyone or did you see anywhere or hear anywhere in the text of the announcement itself that it only applied to one particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an order, if my memory serves me right. And it definitely applied to everyone. It applied to all the places where people had set up or were in the process of setting up barricades across the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that something like this, let's call it an order, applied to military units? Were military units ever being given orders in this form?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any such thing. I'm certain I never heard anything like that. And I don't think this would have been possible. The general headquarters are the commanders of the army. They have their own methods of work and laws which they have to follow in their work. They even have military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that any order was ever issued to the police in this same way?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. The police are under the jurisdiction of the Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP, and they must follow the same rules as in the old times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I can quote the exact line. I do have it written down somewhere. Page 14, line 10. At any rate, you were speaking about the proceedings against Mr. Kurnoga or Mr. Sidjak. You said someone had interceded or intervened, a person from the leadership of the state at that time. Why was there intercession or intervention? Do you remember what the reason for this intervention was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an intervention from the very top of the state. That's what I said. But this was related to the removal of Mr. Kurnoga from his position as the president of the municipality. I may not be accurate when I say that it was towards the end of 1994, but I know that it was in the autumn of 1994. The whole leadership of Republika Srpska was in Prijedor, and I think that there was an electoral campaign. Mr. Radovan Karadzic, we had a meeting with citizens of Prijedor at the mine, and then Karadzic went to the municipality building where they discussed this. And I only heard later that that was when and where Mr. Kurnoga had been removed, but I was not myself present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said on page 31, line 17 that the SNS party asked from you to give them 2.000 German marks, and that's one of the reasons why you were removed, namely, you didn't want to give them the money.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but that happened in 1998. And I dare say that it is a customary practice among the majority of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of that party at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 32 to 34, you were talking about refuelling the cars at the time when there was no petrol to be had. His Honour Schomburg wanted to know how you went about refuelling your cars. I would, therefore, like to ask you a few questions about that. Were you, as a company, owners of some petrol stations?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ljubija mines is not the owner of the petrol stations, and we had two -- I apologise. Every production floor had a petrol station, Omarska, Tomasica, and the central mine. All of the three had petrol stations. When these facilities were being constructed, the mines also constructed the petrol stations, but the mines handed over the petrol stations to Energopetrol which was a state-owned company. We were obliged to refuel our cars there, petrol stations, and we had to pay for that petrol. However, these petrol stations were manned by our own employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you the owners of the fuel that was to be found at these petrol stations?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At these petrol stations, was fuel sold to other citizens, or was it for your own purposes and for nobody's purposes but your own?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not sell fuel to other people because we were not registered with the court register as traders in oil and petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 38, line 2, you were talking about your new ID and whether you know if IDs were being issued in Cirkin Polje. You said that you don't know. Where did you have to go to obtain your new ID?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: ID as a document has always been obtained from the MUP; before the war, during the war, and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain your ID from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the pass that served to enable you to move during the curfew, where did you get that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the exhibit marked S180, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please, in order to save time, just one question related to the present document, this is S308. May I ask you, have you seen this document ever before, the one you have before you in the moment? S308, if Mr. Usher can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember ever having seen this document, but even if it had reached the mine, and I believe it did, it would have been forwarded to the accounting services or to the finance sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it was directed to the managers of enterprises, other organisations, but it would be your testimony it never reached your level of management. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat: The mail that arrives in the service that handles all the mail which is a part of the legal department. This particular service handles all the mail and distributes the mail to the relevant addressees. There were many such documents, and it is even possible that this may have reached me, that it may have been in my hands once. But I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please answer with a clear yes or no. Did you ever receive or read yourself conclusions or orders signed by Dr. Stakic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Number 29, please. It's page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, can you open this document on page 42. You will see number 29 on the top of that page. This order was issued on the 16th of June, 1992. Did you manage the petrol station in Omarska after the 27th and the 28th May, 1992, when, as you testified, the army and the police had taken over the facilities in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the army and the police entered your facilities in Omarska, who was it who managed the petrol station in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm sure it wasn't us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 47 of today's transcript, line 1, we were talking about the legality of the takeover in Prijedor Municipality. I would like to go back a bit further, a bit further back, in October 1991 and the period after October 1991. And I would like to ask you the following: The assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was it able to work legally without representatives of the Serbian people? What is your opinion? I know that you are not an expert, but what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't work given all the laws about the three peoples that constitute the assembly and the state. So my logic tells me that it couldn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a position to work legally without the chosen representatives of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same. Again, it couldn't work legally because it was supposed to consist of all the three state-forming peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The enactment issued by Alija Izetbegovic by which he proclaimed himself president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although such a position at that time was not envisaged by the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was this enactment a legal enactment or an illegal enactment? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was not legal. It was contrary to the law because it should have been the presidency that was supposed to run Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you think as a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, are the principles of legality and legitimacy, were they abandoned long before the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I follow the work of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I could see that there was no agreement among the representatives. And it became clear to me that the result, the outcome, would be what eventually was. And already at that time, one could see that there was no legitimacy in the work of the representatives. So to my opinion, the laws had been abandoned long before that. It is my opinion as a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 52, line 4, and this is going to be my last question, His Honour Schomburg asked you whether you were interested in what was happening in your facilities in Omarska, whether you carried out any investigation into that. I'm going to ask you the following: Did you have any authority whatsoever to investigate actions, documents by the Ministry of the Interior and the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do it. There was no way I could do that. I already mentioned earlier this morning that I had a conversation with Mr. Simo Drljaca, and we talked about the person that I wanted to have released from the investigation centre. If I had pursued that, I would have lost my life, my life was at stake if I had pursued that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's a fact. But legally, under the law, did you have the right to investigate into the doings of the police and the military at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any rights whatsoever to do that. I didn't have any legal authority to do that. I was not in the position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something that didn't enter the transcript. Can you please repeat what you said about the statute.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of my authorities and the way I worked was regulated by the statute of the iron ore mines Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Marjanovic. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Any questions in recross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, two areas, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please: Further cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked just now by Mr. Lukic about the telegram of the 29th of April from the interior minister, purported telegram Delimustafic, instructing the police and Territorial Defence to stop the JNA from leaving Bosnia. And you mentioned that telegram the first day you testified. You are aware, are you not, that that telegram -- that the authenticity of that telegram was denied by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina the next day? Correct? Either the 29th or the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was denied. I saw the document when I came here, and this is a document referred to in the announcement that was broadcast on the 30th of April. That document which was signed by Mr. Delimustafic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On Monday, on page 30 of the transcript on line 18, you talked about this telegram. And you said: "I have heard about this document from my conversations with my associates. I have even heard that this document happened to fall into the hands of the leadership and the Serbian people." First, can you tell us which associates told you about this telegram?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My associates from my company, from the mines, my directors of production floors and sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you have these conversations with your colleagues? The day of the telegram or a different day?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, after the announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This telegram instructing the police to attack the JNA and to prevent the JNA from leaving Bosnia that you saw Monday was addressed to the chiefs of the CSB. Do you know that Stojan Zupljanin was the chief of the CSB for Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The telegram was addressed to the Prijedor -- to all SJBs, and in Prijedor, the chief of the communications of the SJB was Milos Jankovic, a man of Serbian ethnicity. Did you know him and were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said on Monday that you heard this document had fallen into the hands of the leadership and the Serbian people, that would indicate to me, and you can correct me, that the document was attempted -- that someone had attempted to keep it secret from the leadership and the Serbian people. Would you agree that if a document is sent to Mr. Zupljanin and a document is sent through Mr. Milos Jankovic, both of Serbian ethnicity, and Mr. Zupljanin, an SDS member and later on the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region, that this document could hardly have been intended to be secret from the Serbian people if it was authentic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, and what I've told you was based on the stories that I heard on the conversations that I had with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I understand your knowledge is limited on that subject. I want to go, then, finally you were asked by Mr. Lukic your opinion today about the legality of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if I understand your answer, you believed that that assembly became illegal when the SDS deputies or the Serbian deputies who constituted a minority but represented one people walked out of that assembly and it continued without the Serbian people. You've also told us that you believe that the Prijedor assembly of Dr. Stakic, the president was Dr. Stakic, was legal although two nationalities who constituted a majority of the people of Prijedor were excluded. Can you reconcile for me why you believe it's illegal for Bosnian assembly to continue without the participation of the Serbian people, but it was legal in Prijedor to throw out the majority of deputies of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these two things are beyond comparison. The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I cannot interpret because I'm not a legal expert, but I believe that it regulates that there are three state-forming peoples and the presidency. As to the work of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor is that decisions are taken by a simple majority as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked a question today by Mr. Lukic, and I'm sorry, I don't quite quickly enough to get all of the question, but I believe I correctly wrote down part of your answer, whether or not -- wasn't it true that legality had been abandoned long before the 30th of April. And your answer in part was: "So in my opinion, the laws had been abandoned long before that." So is it correct, sir, that in your opinion, what you saw the government of Dr. Stakic, the government that was ruling Prijedor after the takeover, was ruling a state or was ruling territory no longer governed by law but governed by force?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions about the work of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina I derived from television. I didn't say that I knew anything about that. But in any case, the assembly was more like a theatre. And since not all the sessions were broadcast on television, I was not in the position to be aware of all the conclusions made by that assembly. But in any case, towards the end of its work, the assembly looked more like a theatre than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we -- there was a misunderstanding, and I get it from the line of questions put to you by Mr. Lukic. My question indeed was not before the break whether you had any right or any possibility to investigate with the assistance of documents of the Ministry of the Interior or the MUP. My question was, and therefore, I repeat it: Did you ever try to get access to the area of Omarska, part of your enterprise? Did you ever try to go there and to verify what happened there in the period of time between the 1st of May and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't try because I was afraid. I admit that publicly, I feared for my life. And I believe that I've already told you that I have a family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness just briefly Exhibit S395. May it be put on the ELMO because we don't have an English translation. Would you briefly summarise what you can see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document based on which oil and petrol was sold in Omarska. Here, I can see the date. Here I can see the names of the people who were in charge of various machines. Here I can see the type of machine. Also I can see what kind of fuel has been sold. And the quantity of the fuel sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Excuse me, Your Honour, it's in the transcript this document, page 67, line 23, that it's about selling. This gentleman never mentioned sale of oil. He said "manipulation," so you may ask him to explain if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you once again - maybe it is a question of interpretation - what can be seen in column number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see figures, 50, 20, 30, and so on and so forth. I assume because it says "oil" here, this must be litres of oil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be in line with your testimony that there were separate petrol stations, here the one in Omarska. You mentioned already beforehand TAMici or TAM. Did you ever hear that there was a theft of fuel or that fuel was illegally sold in Omarska to third persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say, but here I don't see any signature. I wouldn't dare say that this was all done legally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can see the list of the names. To the best of your recollection, do you know one of these persons listed in column 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the person under number 7, Branko Kicema.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you meet this person later on after 1992, Branko Kicema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. And I still meet him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him what was the purpose - apparently he was a driver or refuelled the TAM with the plate number PD59 or 545-46.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not talk to him. And as for this document, I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I absolutely understand this. But it's dated the 2nd of June, 1992. And following your statement, at this time, the ore mine as such was no longer operational. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already explained, the petrol station in the part of the surface excavation was still in operation because that took maintenance. There was a shortage of electricity and there were people operating the generator. So I cannot claim that Kicema Branko was taking this petrol to the generator, to use the petrol for the generator, but I know that the petrol station was in operation the whole time. I know because one of the directors had told me that it had not been flooded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you the following last question: Did you ever discuss with Branko Kicema whether or not - and this is alleged here in this case - this TAM with this plate number was used to carry dead bodies away from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never heard this before, and I certainly never discussed anything like this with Branko Kicema.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Any other questions by any parties? I have to thank you very much for coming to The Hague to testify. I know it was extremely difficult for you, nearly an entire week, and under your special health conditions. But I believe you have assisted us in coming closer to the truth. I wish you a safe trip home and all the best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, if I may, will you please allow me to say the following: I want to offer my apologies to all those for whom I have created problems with my quick speech or my inaccurate phrasing. I really hope that my testimony will assist you to shed light on the whole matter, and I must say this again. I only spoke the truth and nothing but the truth. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you. And please have a safe trip. May the usher please escort the witness out of the courtroom. And if there are no impediments, please at the same time escort the next witness into the courtroom. This would be number 79. May I ask the Defence, is there any request for any protective measure?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to this witness, Your Honour, there are not, but we do have one issue that the witness will touch upon, as identified in our proffer, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could remain outside for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You are called as a Defence witness, and therefore the floor is yours, Mr. Ostojic. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic, we represent Mr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions here this afternoon, and I'd like as a preliminary matter to suggest to you that if you do not understand my question or would like me to clarify further, that you please state so and I will attempt to do the best I can to rephrase my question. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me begin, sir, by asking you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Milan Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: 24th of October, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For purposes of some personal background, can you share with us your marital status.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I am married. I am married. I have two children, a daughter and a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you presently reside?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Currently I reside in Omarska, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when you say "Omarska," sir, there has been some generalizations made by various individuals that identify Omarska as the iron ore mine. Omarska is a town, is it not, within the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Omarska is a town with about a thousand households. The iron ore mine is about 2 and a half or 3 kilometres away from where I live, or more specifically from the settlement itself. So the town is one thing, and the mine's quite another. And it's a certain distance away from the settlement itself, and it stands within its own perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, sir, where you lived in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I lived in Omarska, and I still reside in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same place where you live today, correct, sir? The same home, same distance away from the iron ore mine. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I have been in the same place since 1967 to this very day. We have a family house. That's where I reside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking you, but can you tell us please what your ethnic background is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, sir, briefly your educational background by telling us the highest level of education that you attained, where, and when.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I went to elementary school, eight years of elementary school, eight grades. I completed the eight grades in Omarska. And then in 1963, I went to Slovenia. It was a secondary school for construction engineers. And then after that, I went to do my regular military service for the JNA. After I returned from my military service, I went to a higher school -- a high college for construction engineers in 1971. And that was also -- that was an associate degree in construction engineering. And that was also the last academic experience that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can just share with us briefly your employment history starting with graduation in 1971. Just a brief overview, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I came to Banja Luka, and I worked for a construction company. It was called Granica. We were building a hospital. I stayed in that company until 1978. In 1978, more specifically in the spring of 1978, I went for a while to Canada where I stayed for three years. Upon my return in 1981, I renovated my family home. And in 1982, I found a job with the communal services and administration in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your testimony, is it, sir, that in 1982 you became employed by the Department of Communal Services and you continue to this day to be employed in such a capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since 1982, I have been with the communal services. However, the name of the communal services back then was the 4th of July until the beginning of the war in Bosnia. And then I think the name was changed in 1993. The name was Kongrad. Now it's called communal services. But it still has the same function. It still has the same tasks. It's only that different managing directors who came always changed the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, is this -- if you can tell us, having been there in excess of 20 years, is this Department of Communal Services a department that falls within the civilian organs, the MUP organs, Minister of Interior, or the military organs in the Prijedor Municipality during the time period that you, sir, have worked there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Communal services which does general sanitation work across Prijedor Municipality which includes Omarska, Kozarac, those were the major settlements, and Ljubija, too, always fell within the civilian organs. The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly had the authority over it, or more specifically, its own branch for communal services.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to come back in some detail with respect to your duties and obligations specifically related to the spring and summer of 1992. However, let me ask you some general questions. In 1990 and 1991, were you, sir, at all times a resident of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: All the time. I lived in Prijedor Municipality, or more specifically, in my family house in Omarska. It's a house I own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. During that entire period of time, sir, can you share with us your personal experiences and observations with respect to whether there was a voluntary exodus of citizens of Prijedor, meaning that they are leaving the Prijedor Municipality in the time period of 1990 and 1991? Share with us that which you personally experienced and observed.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing I can say is that as early as 1990, after the multiparty elections, which we had never had prior to that in the former Yugoslavia, as early as 1991, you could feel a certain insecurity among people belonging to any of the different ethnic groups. After the 1990 elections, there was a lot of uncertainty and insecurity in 1991. So I don't think I have anything special to add to that. You could tell that people were confused by the facts surrounding them. In the autumn of 1991, you could tell that ranks of Muslims were forming.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Queues were forming of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Women and children were standing in queues in order to obtain passes, I think. As during my time in my job when I was doing the sanitation rounds as an inspector, I did notice these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also, sir, prior to April 30th, 1992, notice an influx of Serbian refugees coming from Croatia as a result of the war that had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: There was quite a considerable influx from Croatia. Large numbers of people from Prijedor Municipality who were originally from Prijedor Municipality were working temporarily across the border in Croatia. So that as early as 1991, many people came back. Perhaps even about 90 per cent of all the people who had been working in Croatia. They were returning to stay with their relatives, and then whole families started returning. So there was a significant increase in the population of the town of Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I would just ask counsel, I've rethought the issue that we discussed in private session, and perhaps we will get to that after the break and we can talk about it over the break. I just want to warn counsel I would like to rediscuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One of the agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm merely nodding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me specifically what -- so that we have a better idea and appreciation of what it is that you did in terms of your employment at the communal services, share with us specifically what your duties and obligations were in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see you addressed your question to Mr. Ostojic, and actually my name is Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is actually -- that's fine. I'll restate the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, there was a mistake with the interpretation when they identified me as the speaker, and it may have been confused the witness. If I can just be permitted to restate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, can you tell us with some specificity what your duties and obligations were as an employee of the communal services in the spring and summer of 1992 so that we may better have an appreciation of the tasks and that which you performed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: During 1991, my duty was general sanitation work in the town of Prijedor, the care and maintenance of green areas, the collection of garbage throughout the area, and then if there had been heavy precipitations, we would have to clean the manholes and grilles. We were in charge of the pavements of the Prijedor town and of the green areas. I had a number of people working under me. I was some sort of a foreman for these particular tasks and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's break that down if you don't mind. Can you tell us how many employees were employed with the department of communal services at or about the time at issue?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, we had about 130 employees. They were distributed in several work units. There was sanitation, there was the green areas unit. We had a cemetery unit, people who were in charge of maintaining cemeteries. We had workshops where our machines were maintained and repaired. And then I think under the patronage of the same company, we had the water supplies section, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned also, sir, that you were a foreman and that you had employees working under you. Can you share with us during that time period the number of employees that worked under you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I had about 25 people under me, people that did the work that I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And me just break this down for the time frame because it's critical for us, and I appreciate your understanding of this, sir. I'm going to ask you prior to April 30th, 1992, did you have approximately 25 people working under you at the department of communal services?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Between 25 and 30, I would say, then, which is still the case today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate your answer. But let me break it down a little further. From the period of April 30th through September 1992 how many people were employed with you or working under you in the department of communal services?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, depending on the exact point in time, between 20 and 25. Between April and -- well, for the entire period of time you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did during this period of time, specifically April through September of 1992, did you have employees who worked under you in the department of communal services of ethnic backgrounds other than Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were Muslims working there. We had Croats working there, too. There were Roma people working there, too. There were different ethnic backgrounds represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, from April 30th through September 30th, 1992, did at that time these different ethnic groups, the Muslims, Croatians, and other non-Serbs continue to maintain their employment at the department of communal services?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They still work there today. A number of those people who were working there at that point have already retired by now, but new people came. We still have different ethnic backgrounds in our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time as a foreman obtain or receive an order to discharge non-Serbs, Muslims, or Croatians from the department of communal services during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, no. We received no such order from anyone, and we didn't do any such thing. We did not dismiss anyone. We were short of manpower anyway, so we certainly would not have dismissed any of the people who did work for us. It was very difficult to get manpower, to hire new people or to find new people to hire. So we kept the minimum and tried to keep the whole thing working.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the extent possible, and I recognise I am taxing your memory, can you list for us by way of example the names of some of those Muslims, Croatians, and non-Serbs who worked in the department of communal services and who were not discharged during the period of April through September 1992? I would be grateful --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps... Mario Zombra, a Croat; Mile Ivankovic; Stipo Saric. Then there was also a number of Muslims, Ibrahim Redic. Djakovic [phoen], he was a Roma person; Dzevad Karabic; Mesud Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you think of any others from time to time, just feel free to share it with us. Sir, I'd like also to have a better appreciation and understanding of the department of communal services in its entirety. I'd like to know who was the director in the spring and summer of 1992 of this department of communal services.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The director of the 4th of July communal company in the summer of 1991 and throughout 1991 up to July 1992 was Jusuf Harambasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, what the ethnic background is of Mr. Jusuf Harambasic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, because it concerns us particularly, because it falls within the period of the fourth amended indictment, is it your testimony that Mr. Jusuf Harambasic continued to work as the director of the Department of Communal Services through the period of April 30th, 1992, up through and including July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jusuf Harambasic discharged in July of 1992, or did he voluntarily leave his post?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: He voluntarily left his post. He said himself that he could no longer discharge the duties, and then he was replaced by Mr. Milanko, Dujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Share with me the hierarchy, if you will, who appoints the director such as Jusuf - I forget his last name already - Harambasic to work with the Department of Communal Services and who can discharge that individual? Who can fire him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: He was appointed -- first, there is an opening, and candidates are invited to apply for the position. And then the best candidate is chosen according to the prescribed rules and conditions set forth by the company. So that person has to have a certain qualification, and all the other things. My company was like any other. This is a service company that performed tasks and had a role that it had. It is not a political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, sir, and forgive me for asking the questioning. And I apologise because it was not specific enough for your complete understanding. My question, sir, however is with respect to this Mr. Jusuf Harambasic, who is it, sir, that he would apply to in order to get a job? Did he go to the MUP building, for example, to get a job? Did he go to the military to get a job? Would he go to the Municipal Assembly to get a job? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, that is, the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. That was the body that could appoint him because the body that my company reported to was the municipality or, in other words, the Executive Board which was in charge of the work of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear, sir, and have a complete appreciation for that, could the president of the Municipal Assembly, even prior to April of 1992, could he appoint an individual to be director of the Department of Communal Services? Or was it exclusively -- exclusively the right of the Executive Board to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board, because the Executive Board was in the position to remove people. The Executive Board can initiate that. Employees also can initiate that, but it is the Executive Board that makes decisions on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, specifically with your performance of your duties and obligations as an employee of the Department of Communal Services, would you have an occasion, sir - and tell us the regularity of that occasion, if any - to come to the city/town of Prijedor to perform your tasks and services?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I was there every day. I would work in the town of Prijedor every day. My working hours were between 7.00 in the morning and 3.00 in the afternoon. Sometimes I would stay even longer than that. So I was in Prijedor every day. I went to work there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, how did you travel to the city/town of Prijedor which is within the Prijedor Municipality prior to April of 1992? What was your mode of transportation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I commuted in my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Immediately or during the period of April 1992, to the best of your knowledge, were the trains and buses in operation that worked on a regular basis so that they would provide you public transportation to go from your home in Omarska to the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: After April, there weren't any -- I don't know the exact timetable. Before April, there were. But then around the 30th of April and later on in May, June, July, I'm not sure. There was no public transportation. There were no buses. And as far as I can remember, there were no trains either. I drove in my own cars, and I heard that there were no buses and there were no trains running at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But before taking the break, we have to resolve one issue. Taking into account what has been discussed during our last 65 ter (i) meeting, we would have the possibility to sit tomorrow in the morning from 9.00 to a quarter to 2.00 instead of a quarter past 2.00 to 7.00. Is it convenient for all the parties to move to the morning session?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have scheduled a meeting with Dr. Stakic at 11.00. I'm sure we could reschedule that for 3.00. So with respect to that, it may cause a problem for us because we're not sure if we could get access at that late hour. Secondly, we've reserved a meeting with our witness for tomorrow until tomorrow morning. But I can make some phone calls and see if he would be available to meet in the late hours this evening. If so, then we'll complete that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. Could you please be so kind and give us your final response immediately after the break. From the side of the Prosecution, there seems to be no obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me take the opportunity that it has to be add to the transcript that the Prosecution is now also represented by Ms. Sutherland, and in addition --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to introduce Mr. Halfpenny who is an intern with our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Welcome. The trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask before we start, what about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, if possible the Defence would like to keep the same schedule from 2.15 to 7.00 or whatever the schedule was. If the Court would like to start a little earlier, we would be happy to do that, even as early as 1.00. Only because we would hope to finish by tomorrow night, and our second problem is that the proffer has not been tendered because the witness just flew in and we are going to prepare it this evening, and we would like to give the OTP an adequate opportunity to review that proffer, among other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would say in your words "fair enough." Let's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. try to find out -- but here I don't know whether it would cause any problems related to the lunchtime in the Detention Unit for Dr. Stakic if we would start, say, at 1.00. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Based on the -- based on the detention rules, he will be able to have a meal prior to his departure. And I would assume he would depart at about 12.30, and he would be able to get a meal at 11:30 or so. And I would just move my schedule and meeting with him. We are now presently set to meet at 11.00. But to that extent, we can accommodate the Court, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's in the interests of the waiting witnesses. May I ask Madam Registrar to find out what is possible, especially related to all the people working for us, and first of all making us understand each other, if possible. If you could tell me as soon as possible what will be the outcome. So the preference would be to start at 1.00, and to go until 7.00. If not possible, we would start a quarter past 2.00 as scheduled and go on until 7.00 because I think the reasons given by the Defence are convincing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, I think out of an abundance of caution, we should perhaps have this last bit of discussion redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And to be of further assistance to the OTP, I'll not only concur, but I'll also ask the Court the prior mention of that be redacted. I'm not sure that was in open session, because I think we went into private when we identified that individual by his pseudonym. But for the protection of the witness and also as a courtesy to the OTP, if that can be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If this could be done, it would be very helpful. So this would cover page 86 in part, and we have to return I don't know to which page when the pseudonym and the name of this person was mentioned. So this should be redacted, if Madam Registrar could be of assistance. I thank her in advance. So please. Just to be on the safe side, we are in public session, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, for my purposes. I apologise, Your Honour. I thought the question was directed at the Madam Registrar. For our purposes, we would like to proceed in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, then we proceed in public session. And the floor is yours, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, Mr. Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try if possible to cover some other essential points. And forgive me if I jump around a little bit, but I'll try in my question to give you preparatory time period in which I'd like to discuss with you. But before I begin I'd like to lay the foundation in connection with the following series of questions, and that is, sir: Can you tell us whether or not you know the gentleman by the name of Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, Mr. Rosic, how is it that you know him very well?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I know him for a long time, and there are a number of reasons for which I know him. I married his aunt, his father -- that is, Dr. Milomir Stakic's grandfather and my wife's father were brothers. That's the first reason. And second reason is that after graduation, for a long time, he lived as a tenant very near me. Actually, he was my first-door neighbour. He was a tenant with a lady there. We were friends. We were -- we are related. So that's how I know him so well. In 1991, when he was elected the vice-president, he commuted with me when he went to work in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you raised the issue, can you tell us, sir, with what regularity Dr. Stakic accompanied you when you would go to work in the city/town of Prijedor, during the time period that he was vice-president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Almost every day when he couldn't go to Prijedor, then he wouldn't travel with me. But for as long as he was vice-president, all the time we commuted to work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I know you mentioned what your mode of transportation was during that time period. But just so that I wouldn't ask you a leading question and being presumptuous, share with us what the mode of transportation was when Dr. Stakic accompanied you to the city/town of Prijedor, on a regular and continuous basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Every morning while he was vice-president, every morning I would get up. I would get into my car. And at half past 7.00, we would head for Prijedor. That's what we did in the morning. But he didn't return with me because sometimes he would stay longer. He had a different work routine. So I wouldn't drive him back home. But since we're friends, since we're related, I would give him a lift in the morning so that he didn't have to take a bus or a train. I went to work to Prijedor every day. I had my car, and I gave him a lift regularly every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the mode of transportation was by vehicle, by car. And it was your car that you would take with Dr. Stakic every day to the city/town of Prijedor, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That was my own personal vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you know, why Dr. Stakic didn't take his own mode of transportation or his own vehicle to the city/town of Prijedor, while he was vice-president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Because he didn't have his own car. Dr. Stakic comes from a rather poor family. He was very young when he graduated from the school of medicine and became a physician. When he started working, his salary was not very high, so he worked. He got married. He had a lot of expenses, and he simply couldn't afford his own car. I helped him out by giving him a lift. I told him for as long as I go, you will go with me. Even during his free time, if he needed a car on Saturday or on Sunday to visit his parents who lived some 4 kilometres away from Omarska, I would loan him my car so he could go there. He couldn't use his own car for a simple reason: He didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate your patience on these issues, and forgive me for asking some of the details although perhaps obvious. Sir, how far is the town in which are from and the town that Dr. Stakic is from, how far is that in relation to the city/town of Prijedor in which you drove Dr. Stakic every day?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: 23 kilometres exactly from my house to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, share with us how far your house was in the spring -- prior to April 1992, how far your house was from that of Dr. Stakic's.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The distance was the same from my [as interpreted] house to my house was about 4 to 5 metres. We all practically shared the same courtyard. His entrance and my entrance were 4 to 5 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, how long would it take you to go from your home to the city/town of Prijedor, during the time period in which you drove Dr. Stakic? In minutes, how long would it take?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Usually it took us about 20 to 25 minutes. But we always left at half past 6.00 to be in our respective workplaces at 7.00. 25 minutes is a -- is the minimum of time that it took. But we left half an hour earlier to be on the safe side, to be in our workplace on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that time period, sir, did you have an opportunity to discuss numerous issues with Dr. Stakic in the car, you and Dr. Stakic alone?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: We talked, of course. We talked. We got on well, and we talked about all sorts of things. It depended on our mood and the topic of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did there come, sir, a time in which you ceased giving Dr. Stakic a ride, as you described yourself, being a neighbour, a friend, and also a relative by marriage? Did there come a time, sir, that you stopped giving Dr. Stakic a ride to the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Share with us --
