utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The time came on the 30th of April, 1992. Like every morning, I got up, I got into my car. I turned the engine on, and I waited for him to join me for a ride to Prijedor. He was already a few minutes late when I decided to go and ring his bell. His wife Bozana answered the door and told me: "Miso left with the police some 20 minutes ago." I asked her what had happened. She said, "Nothing really." And from that time on, I didn't give him a ride. So it was on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that day specifically in a moment; however, I have a couple questions. Immediately prior to the 30th of April, 1992, when you ceased giving Dr. Stakic a ride to the city/town of Prijedor, prior to that time, meaning in essence, April 29th, 28th, 27th, and 26th, sir, did you have an occasion to give Dr. Stakic a ride as you have done in the past to the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All these days I gave him a ride to Prijedor. It came as a surprise to me that I did not give him a ride on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, sir, prior to April 30th, meaning the time period immediately before that in which you gave Dr. Stakic a ride to the city/town of Prijedor, do you recall that whether or not Dr. Stakic -- strike that. Do you recall what Dr. Stakic's disposition was?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I did not notice anything unusual. He behaved just like every other day. I did not see -- I didn't notice that he was more tense than usual. Just like any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any nervousness or anxiousness prior -- during the time period prior to April 30th, 1992, that we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't notice anything. On the contrary, in the afternoon, we socialised. We were joking around with his aunt, who is at the same time my wife, Milka. We couldn't notice anything unusual about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did at any time Dr. Stakic prior to the 30th of April share with you any purported theory of a plan for a takeover of Prijedor on April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, never. He didn't mention any actions that would have anything to do with his job. He didn't express any suspicions. We discussed family matters. I never heard from him advocating any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention if we can to the morning of April 30th, 1992. You started to share with us the fact that you were waiting for Dr. Stakic, and after several minutes - and I apologise that I'm paraphrasing your testimony, but you're welcome to correct me if I'm wrong, you waited for him for several minutes. And then you proceeded to go on his door to determine where he was. And you were at that time approached or saw Dr. Stakic's wife, Mrs. Bozana. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, with as much specificity as you can based upon your recollection, what is it that you told Mrs. Bozana and what did she tell you in response, and tell us where this conversation happened.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I rang the bell. Bozana answered the door. She opened the door. I asked her: "Where is the doctor? Are we going to work or not?" She answered: "Miso left. The police drove him away some 15 or 20 minutes ago." I asked her: "What happened?" She said: "Nothing. Nothing bad happened. Just go on. Do whatever you have to do." That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, proceed to go to the city/town of Prijedor, on the 30th of April, 1992? And can you tell me what it is that you saw or learned on the 30th of April, 1992, when you arrived in the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I went to Prijedor. When I arrived at my company, I heard that there had been a takeover. I was surprised. I didn't know what was taken over, how was it taken over. And then they told me that the police and the army had occupied the municipal building and some other facilities, and then I heard that from my colleagues. I didn't hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who told you that, sir, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: My colleagues at work, Dojcinovic. There were a number of people there. Jusuf Harambasic himself, the director of the company, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, did at any time after April 30th, 1992, you have an opportunity to drive Dr. Stakic to the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No. After that, I didn't. A few days later, I didn't really see him. And then later on, I heard that he had an official driver who drove him around and that he had an official car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, the name of that driver that was officially driving Dr. Stakic around?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Petar Stanar who still works in the municipality as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly - and I apologise because it's perhaps a deviation from the line of questions that I previously said to you - this Mr. Jusuf Harambasic, I think you mentioned that he was of the Muslim ethnic background. Do you know, sir, if he still alive today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is alive. He comes to Prijedor from Sanski Most where he resides. He visited -- he has visited us in the company also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me during the period subsequent or after April 30th, 1992, did you have an opportunity to see or visit with Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, no longer as often as I used to. But I would go to the municipality for my work tasks, and I did meet him once in the corridor, in the hall of the Municipal Assembly. We exchanged the usual questions, how are you doing, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After exchanging those typical pleasantries, did you then, sir, proceed to discuss with Dr. Stakic anything of a personal concern to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. I just asked him how he was doing. And I said: "Well, there's one thing, though, I'd like to ask you about." He said: "My brother has a son. And he said: "Yes, I know." And he said: Because their gardens were facing each other. And I asked him whether he could get the son exempted from military service, and then Dr. Stakic told me: "Look, I'm sorry, but really I have nothing to do with these things, I'm nowhere near in charge of these things, and I don't think I could possibly help you." And then I said: "Well, that's fine. That's all right then." And then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And tell us so that we can have a better understanding, when did this happen in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: It was in the second half of May because he had already moved to Prijedor, so I was no longer seeing as much of him as I used to. In the second half of May, perhaps about the 20th of May, I believe. Although it's very difficult for me to pinpoint the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, to ask you some general questions in connection with your duties and obligations as an employee of the department of communal services, were you, sir, issued any new identification cards or passes after April 30th of 1992, or did you, sir, continue to maintain the same identifications that you had in your possession after April 1992 as you had prior to April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I had the same documents as before. I think in 1995 and 1996, there were no new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So is it fair, sir, that you were not issued any new identification cards or documents following the takeover on April 30th, 1992? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No new identification cards were issued. No ID cards, nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But just if I can raise something with the Court relating to the transcript. On page 95, line 19 through 20, we think the witness said, although I can clarify it if the Court thinks it's necessary, I believe the witness said it was until 1995 and 1996 that they received those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, I apologise for having to go back to some questions. And just to clarify this issue with the identification, when did you obtain new identification cards and documents? What year was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify this issue, and I know I believe you've answered it, the documents that were in your possession prior to April 1992, did you continue to use and have those documents after 1992 up until 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I didn't have any other ID documents and no other documents or cards were being issued. So the old ones I had been using them up to 1996, and it was only in 1996 that I was issued a new ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise for asking this. It is relevant for our purposes, however. Were you issued subsequent to April 30th, 1992, any additional identification cards because you were a person of Serbian ethnic background? Or did you continue to simply have the exact same identifications, they weren't changed, and you didn't receive any additional documents or identification papers?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I was only using my old documents. I didn't have any additional cards or documents. Even nowadays, I still have the same driving license that was issued to me in 1980-something and it's still valid. The only thing that was changed, I was issued a new ID card in 1996. But aside from that, no other documents or ID cards were changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, sir, during the time period April 30th, 1992, and August of 1992 whether you have a recollection that there was a curfew in place in the city and the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I did hear about it, and yes, it had been introduced. But I couldn't give you the exact time frame. Probably, yes, in the period you're referring to. There was a curfew, and all of us who worked, who were employed, were given work assignments or work obligations. It was like a certificate certifying that we were there to work so as to keep the police and the army from taking us under their command. We needed a certificate that we were engaged, that we worked in communal services on very specific tasks. These certificates were being issued by the secretariat for all people's defence, but a list had to be drawn up with the names of people one by one. And it made no difference at all whether someone was a Serb, a Muslim, or a Croat. Everyone needed this certificate from the Ministry of Defence in order to be able to move about freely. This, however, didn't apply to the curfew. During the curfew, only persons carrying special passes issued by the Ministry of the Interior or the police were free to move about. Personally, I was never in possession of any such special documents, nor have I ever seen any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You covered a lot of areas and I'd like to clarify if I may. You mentioned this work obligation. Can you tell us, sir, to the best of your recollection when the work obligation initially commenced.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The work obligation was introduced as early as June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Whether it was in June or perhaps as early as May, I don't think I'm able to remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can appreciate that. Can you share with us, sir, since you were a foreman as you identified yourself in the Department of Communal Services, in the spring and summer of 1992 but more specifically after April 30th of 1992, whether the Muslim, Croatian, and non-Serbs who specifically work under you were also given the paperwork and the work obligation so that they could go to work on a daily and regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everyone, that's what I said. No distinction was made as regards the ethnic backgrounds of the employees. The managing director drew up a list containing just the number of people that was sufficient for our company to continue to operate. Sanitation work, garbage collection, maintenance of green areas and parks, mowing the lawns, general sanitation work. It didn't matter what your nationality was. All that mattered were your qualifications, your work specialty. All that was -- all we needed to know was whether you were a driver, whether you were a lawn mower. It was only about people's qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to know and again address and you anticipated my question with respect to permits that may have been issued following -- or outside the hours of the curfew. As Dr. Stakic's neighbour, friend, and relative, did you, sir, obtain any authorisation to have access and to go out outside of the hours imposed by the curfew?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I think I've just said that I received a permit for work from the Ministry of Defence, but this did not apply to the hours of the curfew. If I had wanted to apply for that, I would have had to go through an official channel through my company and request such authorisation from the Ministry of the Interior. So the ministry for all people's defence was in charge of issuing the work obligation. These are two different secretariats, opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back now to Dr. Stakic, if we can, and you having not only driven him and as you have testified being a friend, relative, and neighbour. Sir, can you tell us if at any time Dr. Stakic exhibited any hatred towards any ethnic group, specifically Muslims, Croatians, or any other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I can testify with absolute conviction, and I do know Dr. Stakic very well and I've known him for a very long time, both him and his family, his father, his mother, his brother. I know all of them. I knew what kind of family they are. I know what sort of people they are. I have never heard him utter a word of hate, not a single word. He never talked about Serbs as a separate thing in terms of Serbs being good and Muslims being bad, Croats being bad. I've never heard him utter a single word along these lines. And we never discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Having known Dr. Stakic for the period of time that you described, do you know if he had any prejudices or preconceived prejudices or ill will against Muslims, Croats, and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, it is my firm belief that he never did. There was no need for him to harbour any such ill feelings or prejudices, or even to think anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I recognise you know his parents, Dr. Stakic's parents as well, and his brother as well as his wife. Can you share with us if any members of Dr. Stakic's immediate family, including his wife, parents, and brother, ever exhibited any signs of hatred, ill will, prejudice, or discrimination against Muslims, Croats, and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I certainly never heard them or saw them do anything like that, or harbour any such feelings. We go back a long way. Dr. Stakic's family or his relatives, they are not very political people. So it is my deepest conviction that they never harboured any ill feelings against any group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question since you raised the issue of politics: Do you know whether in 1991 or 1992 Dr. Milomir Stakic was a member of a party called the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that because he was in Omarska. That's where he resided. And he was a local candidate of the party at the elections. So yes, I did know even at a very early stage, I was aware of that. That was before the elections in 1990. He was elected. He got the votes, and he left and assumed the position of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just correct me if I'm wrong, sir, but unfortunately and quite frankly unintentionally, there may have been some liberties taken with the name of this party. But the party's full name, is it not, sir, is the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic. The people's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like ask you, sir, some questions in connection with the date specifically of May 30th, 1992. Can you share with us, sir, to the best of your recollection what if anything occurred on May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: The 30th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know it's late, with the Court's permission if I can just maybe help him on this issue here. It might be a leading question, if that's all right with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have nothing against leading questions. If they are not misleading, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have essentially for our purposes in this trial set the date of May 30th, 1993, [sic] as the time that there was an attack by Muslim extremists on the city/town of Prijedor. Do you remember that event, sir, as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: I remember that event relatively clearly. There were attacks at night. Tukovi in Prijedor was one of the parts, sections of the town attacked. Stari Grad was attacked, too. And there was fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify a couple points. Were you there, sir, in the city/town of Prijedor on May 30th, 1992, when the attack started or at any time commenced?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I think "nee" means no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction and apology.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, I was in Omarska at that time. I was not in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're just having a little bit of -- it's late and I appreciate your patience. Let me ask you this question just so that we're clear for the record again. Sir, were you physically in the city/town of Prijedor on May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Subsequent or after that date, did you have an occasion, sir, to go to the city/town of Prijedor in your capacity as an employee of the Department of Communal Services after the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Not on that day, I didn't go. But on subsequent days, yes, I did go. And I didn't take my usual route, I didn't take the usual route through Kozarac, but rather I took a detour through Maricka, Rakelici, the road for Tomasica and then on to Prijedor. I was scared and I had heard that one couldn't travel through Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, when you arrived in the city/town of Prijedor that which you observed.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I heard and I saw then that there was a riot in Prijedor. There was shattered glass. There were buildings that were damaged. It was a chaos. I couldn't believe my eyes. I couldn't believe that such things had happened, and I couldn't bring myself to believe that any such thing was possible. It was unlike anything I had seen up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who, sir, had the responsibility to clean up the city/town of Prijedor after the attack by, as we have coined them, Muslim extremists on -- after May 30th, 1992? Who is it that picked up the garbage, replaced the glass from the floor and placed -- please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ROSIC
utterances.text: My work unit was collecting the garbage, was cleaning the glass, the shattered glass away. And whatever a man was strong enough to lift in his hands. This took days. There was a lot to be cleaned out. It took us between seven and ten days to deal with this situation. But where major damage had occurred or where parts of buildings had been damaged or collapsed, there was a different unit with their own machines who were dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like now because of the time of the day to go into the matter that we discussed previously in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Will it be time enough that we can conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Would it be time enough to do this in the next seven minutes or would it be more appropriate to do it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe I can finish it. It's really not as lengthy as everyone is anticipating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's go into private session, please.
